In Dutch, the official and widely recognized expression is Jan en alleman, which translates to "everyone" or "any Tom, Dick, and Harry." 
Here is a breakdown of the standard idiom and how your variations fit in: 
1. Jan en alleman (The Original Idiom)
  • Meaning: It is used to refer to a cross-section of society or a large group of willekeurige (random) people. For example, "Dat hoeft Jan en alleman niet te weten" means "Not just anyone needs to know that." 
  • Spelling: According to official spelling rules, Jan must always be capitalized because it refers to the archetypal or fictional person "Jan", historically the most common first name in the Netherlands. 
  • Origin: Historically, the word alleman simply meant "every man" or "everyone". The addition of "Jan" became a humorous popular pairing to make the phrase more descriptive. 
2. Jan-A / Pan-A (Play on Words)
While "Jan-alleman" or "Jan en alleman" represents the standard, everyday person, your inclusion of "Pan-A" or "pan-alleman" appears to be a clever modern play on words. It blends the traditional idiom with contemporary terminology, most likely referencing pansexuality (attraction to people regardless of their gender) combined with alleman (everyone). 
Are you researching this for a specific linguistic context, a creative writing project, or were you looking into the etymology of traditional Dutch "Jan" expressions (like Jan Modaal or Jan met de pet)? Let me know how you would like to proceed!
